extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in democracy, public administration, and political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic criteria and observations for judging how democratic institutions affect public officers, administration, public finance, magistrates' discretion, record-keeping, and salaries. The page offers normative and descriptive standards about stability, remuneration, accountability, and fiscal tendencies under democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability of laws and deliberative delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Change of men must proceed a change of opinions and of measures which forfeits the respect and confidence of nations... Jefferson: 'I think we ought to have obviated it by deciding that a whole year should always be allowed to elapse between the bringing in of a bill and the final passing of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: laws and major measures should be stable and subject to sufficient deliberation (example proposal: a year between introduction and final passage; if expedited, require supermajority such as two-thirds). Rationale: prevent capricious frequent changes that 'poison the blessings of liberty' and erode public confidence. Anti-pattern: rapid, unchecked legislative alteration that reflects transient passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple exterior of public officers / absence of official costume
rubrics_metrics.description: Public officers in the United States are commingled with the crowd of citizens; they have neither palaces, nor guards, nor ceremonial costumes... A public officer in the United States is uniformly civil, accessible to all the world, attentive to all requests, and obliging in all his replies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: the visible humility and accessibility of officers (no ostentatious robes or trappings) as a democratic norm that encourages respect for office over personal exaltation. Guidance notes: modest exterior can strengthen 'manly independence' of citizens; however, the influence of costume may be exaggerated and some ceremonial show can be tolerated if officers are uniformly remunerated. Anti-pattern: ceremonial pomp combined with unpaid offices that produces an aristocratic oligarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remuneration of public officers (paid vs unpaid)
rubrics_metrics.description: All public services, of whatsoever nature they may be, are paid; so that every one has not merely a right, but also the means of performing them... The substitution of paid for unpaid functionaries is of itself... sufficient to constitute a serious revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: whether public offices are remunerated. Guidance: paid offices democratize access (prevent concentration of office among the wealthy) but can signal major constitutional/political shifts; unpaid offices tend to restrict officeholders to the affluent and can lead toward aristocracy. Consider implications for recruitment, representation, and social composition of officeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence (or absence) of a public career and effects of frequent rotation
rubrics_metrics.description: In nations in which the principle of election extends to every place in the state, no political career can, properly speaking, be said to exist... Men are promoted as if by chance... the persons who engage in the perplexities of political life are individuals of very moderate pretensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: continuity and professionalization of public service. Guidance: short terms and frequent turnover limit development of administrative expertise, discourage talented individuals from entering politics, and produce administrations staffed by ordinary men. Anti-pattern: systemic rotation that prevents accumulation and transfer of institutional experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope for arbitrary power of magistrates under democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: In two different kinds of government the magistrates exercise a considerable degree of arbitrary power; namely, under the absolute government of a single individual, and under that of a democracy... the choice of the means is left to their own discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: degree of discretion granted to officials and whether law leaves essential choice of means to magistrates. Examples: New England selectmen drawing jury lists based only on electors and reputation; authority to post names of habitual drunkards and prohibit liquor supply. Guidance: evaluate where legal rules provide detailed prescriptions versus leaving broad discretion, and the risks of arbitrary action when wide discretion is unaccompanied by accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and responsibility mechanisms for magistrates
rubrics_metrics.description: American Editor: 'It is a fundamental principle of our system, that all officers are liable to criminal prosecution whenever they act partially or oppressively from a malicious or corrupt motive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: presence and effectiveness of legal and institutional checks (criminal liability, responsibility to other departments, statutory limits) that distinguish independence from arbitrariness. Guidance: assess whether discretionary powers have prototypes in other systems and whether discretionary measures are accompanied by responsibility and oversight. Anti-pattern: independence without avenues for redress or prosecution for abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability of the administration and preservation of records
rubrics_metrics.description: The public Acts of a Community frequently leave fewer Traces than the Occurrences of a Family... The only historical remains in the United States are the newspapers... But little is committed to writing, and that little is wafted away for ever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: record-keeping, archival practice, and institutional memory as requirements for the 'art of government.' Guidance: administrations should commit decisions, observations, and institutional knowledge to writing and archives so future officeholders can build upon them; anti-patterns include oral/traditionary governance, lack of archives, and discontinuity that impede the cumulative improvement of administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic culture and level of enlightenment required for democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy... always presupposes the existence of a high degree of culture and enlightenment in society... it could only come last in the succession of human history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: evaluate societal education, civic virtue, and public enlightenment as preconditions for a well-functioning democracy. Guidance: democratic institutions function best where citizens are informed and versed in public affairs; absence of such culture undermines administration and leads to poor governance outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of social classes and their fiscal preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Communities... are composed of certain elements... The people may always be mentally divided into three distinct classes: the wealthy; those in easy circumstances; those with little or no property... each of these classes will exercise an influence, peculiar to its own propensities, upon the administration of the finances of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: analyze the class composition of the electorate and predict fiscal policy tendencies accordingly. Guidance: middle-class governments tend to be most economical; governments dominated by the poor tend to increase public expenditure and structure taxes to shift burden to the wealthy; use class proportions to assess likely tax/regulation outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency of democratic governments to increase public expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two striking reasons which show that the tendency of the expenditure will be to increase, not to diminish... the power which lays on taxes escapes the payment of them... the public treasure [can be] exhausted... to relieve indigent citizens, or to supply the games and theatrical amusements of the populace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: anticipate higher public spending in democracies due to (a) majority-rule incentives to benefit voters at others' expense, (b) desire to improve the condition of the poor, (c) feverish appetite for innovations and reforms, and (d) administrative inefficiency causing waste or unfinished projects. Mitigations: greater property ownership among the populace, representative institutions, and constraints on spending can reduce this tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property distribution moderates democratic extravagance
rubrics_metrics.description: The extravagance of democracy is, however, less to be dreaded in proportion as the people acquires a share of property... America, where the great majority of the citizens is possessed of some fortune, is in a still more favorable position than France.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: degree of property ownership among the electorate as a moderating factor on fiscal populism. Guidance: when many citizens hold property, taxes necessary to fund public spending affect broader interests and create resistance to wasteful expenditures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic tendencies in salaries of public officers
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a powerful reason which usually induces democracies to economise upon the salaries of public officers... In America the secondary officers are much better paid, and the dignitaries of the administration much worse than they are elsewhere... the salaries seem to decrease as the authority of those who receive them augments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: distribution of public compensation — democracies tend to raise pay for lower-level/subordinate officers while underpaying high-ranking dignitaries. Guidance: assess salary scales for distortions: democracies may favor parity with the public and penalize visible high pay for principal officers (risking insufficient compensation for senior responsibilities), while competitive private-sector opportunities may require adequate pay for secondary officers. Consider political perceptions (envy, fairness) that shape pay decisions.
